topic: Fraction equivalence and comparison: numerator-only and denominator-only errors

traps.desc: added the same number to the top that was added to the bottom instead of multiplying

problems.slot: (a) numerator of the first fraction in fortieths

traps.desc: replaced the denominator with 40 but left the numerator at 3

problems.slot: (b) numerator of the second fraction in fortieths

problems.desc: Part (d): a correct diagnosis says that with the same numerator, a larger denominator cuts the whole into more, smaller pieces, so three of them is less -- comparing denominators as if they were whole numbers reverses the truth. Full credit requires naming the size of the pieces, not just repeating the corrected sign.

Part (b): a correct diagnosis says the two fractions name the same amount because both the top and the bottom of the first were divided by the same number, 2, which does not change how much of the whole is shaded -- different digits do not mean different amounts. Full credit requires naming the common factor that links the two.

problems.slot: (a) numerator of the first fraction in twelfths

traps.desc: changed only the denominator to 12 and left the numerator at 5

problems.desc: Part (c): a correct diagnosis says that a numerator counts pieces but says nothing about how big a piece is, so 7 small pieces can be less than 5 large ones -- the two fractions have to be rewritten over the same denominator before their numerators can be compared. Full credit requires the idea that the pieces are different sizes.

problems.slot: (c) the true rule, with a reason
problems.desc: Part (c): a correct response states the true rule -- when two fractions have the same numerator, the one with the SMALLER denominator is the larger fraction -- and gives a reason built on piece size: a bigger denominator means the whole is split into more pieces, so each piece is smaller, and the same count of smaller pieces is less. Full credit requires both the rule and the reason.
